library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Computing theoretical diversity from degenerate positions
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: An oligo for a saturation library contains the stretch 5'-...AANDSNRYT...-3', where the degenerate positions are N, D, S, N, R and Y. Which expression gives the theoretical diversity of the library?

choices.B: 4 x 3 x 2 x 4 x 2 x 2

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: Each degenerate code stands for a set of bases: N is any of four, D is three, S is two, R is two and Y is two. The positions vary independently within one molecule, so the number of distinct sequences is the product across positions. A and E add instead of multiplying, which is the single most common error on this kind of question. C assumes every degenerate position is N. D inverts the roles of base count and position count.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Why NNK is used for saturation mutagenesis
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: You are saturating three positions in a protein and your colleague asks why the oligo specifies NNK at each codon rather than NNN. What is the real reason?

choices.A: NNK removes every stop codon from the library.
choices.B: NNK samples all twenty amino acids with fewer codons and only one stop.
choices.C: NNK gives each of the twenty amino acids an equal chance of appearing.
choices.D: NNK is the only degenerate code a DNA synthesizer can produce reliably.
choices.E: NNK restricts the library to the subset of amino acids found in the wild-type protein.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: NNK is thirty-two codons rather than sixty-four. It still encodes all twenty amino acids, but it leaves only one stop codon instead of three, so a smaller library carries a smaller dead fraction. A is the attractive wrong answer: the amber stop survives in NNK. C is false because codon redundancy still differs between amino acids, so leucine and serine remain over-represented relative to methionine and tryptophan. D and E are inventions.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Identifying the step that limits library size
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: You design a degenerate library with a theoretical diversity of about ten to the ninth, amplify it by PCR, ligate it and transform it into competent cells. Which step sets the practical ceiling on how many distinct variants you end up able to screen?

choices.A: The number of PCR cycles used to amplify the degenerate product.
choices.B: The transformation, because the number of colonies bounds the number of distinct clones.
choices.C: The plasmid copy number, because each cell can only hold so many variants.
choices.D: The synthesis scale of the degenerate oligo, which caps the number of sequences made.
choices.E: The sequencing depth used later to check the library.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: The DNA pool coming off a synthesizer and through PCR easily contains far more distinct molecules than the design calls for. What you can actually clone, grow and assay is bounded by how many independent transformants you obtain, which is why library construction is reported in transformants. A is wrong because cycles amplify copies, not variety. C confuses copies per cell with variants per library. D is wrong at any ordinary synthesis scale, which yields picomoles of molecules. E is a measurement made afterward and changes nothing about what the library contains.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Interpreting the coverage requirement for a library
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: For a library of theoretical diversity n, you are told you need roughly 4.6 x n transformants. What does that number mean?

choices.A: It is the number of transformants at which about 99 percent of designed members are present at least once.
choices.B: It is the number of PCR reactions needed to build the library.
choices.C: It is the number of transformants at which every member is present exactly once.
choices.D: It is the fold-excess of oligo over template required during the construction PCR.
choices.E: It is the number of colonies you must sequence to confirm the library.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: Sampling n variants at random into a pool of transformants follows a Poisson distribution, and the chance a given member is missed after sampling k x n times is about e to the minus k. Setting that to one percent gives k of about 4.6. B confuses coverage with construction, which takes one reaction whatever n is. C is impossible, since random sampling never gives a uniform one copy each. D and E attach the number to unrelated steps.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Estimating the missing fraction from the sampling depth
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: Your library has a theoretical diversity of ten thousand and you recover twenty thousand transformants. Roughly what fraction of designed members do you expect to be absent entirely?

choices.A: None, because you collected twice as many colonies as there are members.
choices.B: About half, because colonies are shared between duplicates and new members.
choices.C: About thirteen percent.
choices.D: About one percent, since twice the diversity is the standard coverage target.
choices.E: About eighty-six percent.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: At a sampling depth of k times the diversity, the expected fraction missed is about e to the minus k, and e to the minus two is about 0.135. A is the intuition the Poisson result exists to correct: random sampling piles multiple copies onto some members while missing others entirely. B has no basis. D quotes the right target but the wrong depth, since one percent missing needs about 4.6 x n. E inverts the answer and reports the fraction covered as the fraction missing.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Separating library diversity from the number of reactions
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: You revise a degenerate oligo from two NNK codons to four, raising the theoretical diversity from about a thousand to about a million. How does the number of PCR reactions needed to build the library change?

choices.A: It rises in proportion to the diversity.
choices.B: It rises by a factor of 4.6 to maintain coverage.
choices.C: It does not change; the library is built in one pooled reaction either way.
choices.D: It rises with the square root of the diversity.
choices.E: It falls, because longer degenerate tracts amplify more efficiently.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: A degenerate oligo is a mixture of molecules, so a single reaction containing that mixture produces the whole library at once. Diversity changes what is in the tube, not how many tubes there are. What does scale with diversity is downstream: more transformants for coverage, and more clones or more reads to characterize it. A, B and D all attach the coverage requirement to the wrong step, and E invents a benefit that does not exist.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Distinguishing designed diversity from the library in hand
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: You design a library of theoretical diversity one million, transform it, and count ten thousand colonies on your plates. Your labmate says you have a million-member library because the ligation contains all one million sequences. What is the accurate statement?

choices.A: The library is one million members, since the DNA pool contains them all.
choices.B: The library is ten thousand members, since each colony is one variant you can test.
choices.C: The library is ten billion members, the product of the design and the colony count.
choices.D: The library is one hundred members, the square root of the colony count.
choices.E: The diversity cannot be stated at all without sequencing the pool.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: Both statements about the DNA are true and neither helps: the ligation probably does contain nearly all designed sequences, but what you can screen is the set of clones you actually isolated. Ten thousand colonies is at most ten thousand distinct variants, and in practice fewer because of resampling. A is the error of reporting the design rather than the experiment. C and D combine the two numbers arbitrarily. E overstates the problem, since the colony count already gives a hard upper bound.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Reasoning about bias between designed and realized libraries
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: Your coverage calculation assumes every designed member is equally likely. You then sequence your library and find that variants carrying G at the first degenerate position are three times as common as those carrying T. What does this do to the number of transformants you need?

choices.A: Nothing, because coverage depends only on theoretical diversity.
choices.B: It lowers the requirement, because the library is less diverse than designed.
choices.C: It raises the requirement, because the rarest members now need deeper sampling to appear.
choices.D: It makes the library unusable, since biased libraries cannot be screened.
choices.E: It raises the requirement only if the bias falls inside the coding sequence.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: The 4.6 x n rule assumes uniform sampling. Once some members are systematically rarer, those are the ones that go missing, and you have to sample deeper to be confident they are present. Bias of this kind comes from the phosphoramidite mixture used for the degenerate position and from amplification, and it is why a library is worth sequencing before it is trusted. A ignores the assumption behind the formula. B confuses skew with reduced diversity; the member count is unchanged. D is too strong, since biased libraries are screened all the time. E invents an irrelevant condition.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Reading a construction oligo and computing library size
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: An EIPCR oligo carries the ribosome binding site region 5'-...TTTRVWGGHDTT...-3', with the degenerate positions R, V, W, H and D. What is the theoretical diversity of the resulting library?
library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: R is two bases, V is three, W is two, H is three and D is three, so the product is 2 x 3 x 2 x 3 x 3, which is 108. D is the same product with one of the three-base codes read as two. E treats every position as three-fold. C treats the region as five N positions. B counts the degenerate positions rather than the sequences they generate, which is the error of reporting the design's width rather than its size.

library_diversity_and_coverage.topic: Reconciling coverage requirements with screening capacity
library_diversity_and_coverage.question: You design a library of theoretical diversity five thousand. You can comfortably pick and assay four hundred clones. Which conclusion follows?

choices.A: The screen is adequate, because four hundred clones sample the library randomly.
choices.B: You should reduce the designed diversity, or move to a selection rather than a clone-by-clone screen.
choices.C: You should pick four hundred clones and report the best as the library optimum.
choices.D: You should raise the number of transformants to 4.6 x n, which solves the screening problem.
choices.E: You should sequence the four hundred clones, which recovers the missing members computationally.

library_diversity_and_coverage.explanation: Four hundred clones out of five thousand designed members samples under ten percent of the library, so the best variant is probably never tested. The two honest fixes are to shrink the design so the screen can cover it, or to replace the screen with a selection or sort that handles the whole population at once. A mistakes random sampling for adequate sampling. C is the error of calling a sampled maximum the true one. D fixes coverage of the library in the freezer but not coverage of the assay, which is the binding constraint here. E cannot recover variants that were never assayed.

library_construction_methods.topic: Locating where diversity enters a construction
library_construction_methods.question: You build a promoter library by EIPCR: a pair of primers amplifies the entire plasmid outward from the promoter, and one primer carries degenerate bases in its 5' tail. Where does the diversity in the finished library come from?

choices.A: From errors introduced by the polymerase during the long amplification.
choices.B: From the mixture of molecules in the degenerate primer, copied into every product.
choices.C: From the template plasmid, which must already contain promoter variants.
choices.D: From the ligation, which joins ends in several alternative registers.
choices.E: From the competent cells, which recombine the product after transformation.

library_construction_methods.explanation: A degenerate oligo is not one sequence but a mixture synthesized in parallel, and each molecule in that mixture primes its own product. The library is therefore made at the moment of synthesis and merely carried through the PCR. A describes mutagenesis, which is a different experiment with a far lower and uncontrolled rate. C would require the library to already exist. D and E invent sources of variation that the workflow does not have.

library_construction_methods.topic: Choosing between degenerate synthesis and a defined oligo pool
library_construction_methods.question: You want every single amino acid substitution at each of 250 positions in a protein, with no stop codons and no wild-type carryover. Which synthesis route fits that specification?

choices.A: A degenerate oligo with NNK at every codon, used in one EIPCR reaction.
choices.B: A chip-synthesized oligo pool in which each intended variant is specified individually.
choices.C: Error-prone PCR across the gene at a tuned mutation rate.
choices.D: A degenerate oligo with NNN at every codon, which covers all possibilities.
choices.E: DNA shuffling of the gene against its closest orthologs.

library_construction_methods.explanation: The specification is a defined list, so the synthesis has to be defined too. An oligo pool writes each variant as its own sequence, which is what lets you exclude stops and the wild type and get one substitution per molecule. A and D give random combinations across positions, including multiple substitutions per clone and stop codons, and no control over which members appear. C has no control over position or identity. E recombines existing variation rather than enumerating substitutions.

library_construction_methods.topic: Recognizing Klenow fill-in as a route to a degenerate cassette
library_construction_methods.question: You need a short double-stranded cassette carrying eight random bases, and you have no template containing that region. Two partially complementary oligos are annealed and Klenow is added. What is Klenow doing?

choices.A: Amplifying the annealed pair exponentially, as in PCR.
choices.B: Extending each strand on the other as template to fill the single-stranded overhangs.
choices.C: Cutting the annealed duplex at the degenerate positions.
choices.D: Ligating the two oligos into a closed circle.
choices.E: Removing the random bases to leave a defined sequence.

library_construction_methods.explanation: The two oligos overlap only in part, so annealing leaves recessed 3' ends. Klenow extends from each 3' end using the other strand as template, converting the partial duplex into a full one in a single isothermal step. A is wrong because there is no thermal cycling and no exponential amplification. C, D and E attribute activities to Klenow that belong to restriction enzymes, ligase and nothing at all, respectively.

library_construction_methods.topic: Using overlap extension to place diversity at a junction
library_construction_methods.question: You want a library in which the linker between two protein domains is randomized, and the two domains come from separate plasmids. Why is SOEing a natural choice?

choices.A: It eliminates the need to transform the product into cells.
choices.B: The overlapping primers that join the two fragments can carry the degenerate linker.
choices.C: It raises the theoretical diversity beyond what the degenerate code allows.
choices.D: It avoids the restriction sites that would otherwise appear in the linker.
choices.E: It removes the need to sequence the finished library.

library_construction_methods.explanation: In overlap extension the two fragments are joined through a shared sequence written into the primers, so whatever you put in that shared region ends up at the junction. A degenerate linker is exactly that kind of insertion. A and E are false at any scale. C is wrong because the diversity is set by the code, not the assembly method. D is backwards: SOEing is useful partly because it does not require sites, but the linker's content is a design choice either way.

library_construction_methods.topic: Reading a construction oligo and its tails
library_construction_methods.question: A construction file digests a PCR product with BamHI and EcoRI, and the forward oligo reads GAGTTggatccTTTNVWGGRDTTAAATTatgatggttttccagccaatc. What is the lowercase ggatcc doing?

choices.A: It marks the degenerate region that generates the library.
choices.B: It is the BamHI site, added as a tail so the product can be cut and ligated.
choices.C: It is the ribosome binding site for the downstream gene.
choices.D: It is the annealing region that binds the template.
choices.E: It is a spacer with no function other than setting the product length.

library_construction_methods.explanation: By convention in these files the lowercase runs mark sequence added by the oligo rather than copied from the template, and GGATCC is the BamHI recognition sequence. The GAGTT in front of it is the short flank the enzyme needs in order to cut near the end. A points at the wrong element, since the degenerate region is the NVW and RD stretch. C names the wrong element again. D is wrong because the annealing region is the 3' end that matches the template. E ignores a functional site.

library_construction_methods.question: The pP6 library is built by reassembling a promoter with degenerate sequence at the -35 and -10 boxes while the rest of the promoter is held fixed. Why randomize those two regions rather than the whole promoter?

choices.A: Because synthesis cannot produce degenerate bases outside those regions.
choices.B: Because those boxes are where the polymerase holoenzyme makes contact, so they set strength.
choices.C: Because the regions between them are not transcribed and so cannot matter.
choices.D: Because randomizing the whole promoter would exceed the diversity a single oligo can encode.
choices.E: Because the spacer length between the boxes cannot be varied experimentally.

library_construction_methods.explanation: Sigma factor contacts the -35 and -10 hexamers, so sequence changes there change how readily open complex forms, which is what a promoter strength library is trying to sample. Confining diversity to those positions keeps the library small enough to cover while still spanning a wide range of strengths. A is false. C misstates the biology, since the intervening spacer is part of the promoter and does affect strength. D is a real consideration at some scales but is not the design reason here. E is false; spacer length is a legitimate variable, just not the one varied in this design.

library_construction_methods.topic: Using a position weight matrix to shape a library design
library_construction_methods.question: Instead of putting N at every position of a ribosome binding site, you derive the degenerate code from a position weight matrix built from known functional sites. What does that buy you?

choices.A: It guarantees that every member of the library is functional.
choices.B: It concentrates the library on sequences likely to work, so fewer clones are wasted on dead members.
choices.C: It increases the theoretical diversity for the same oligo length.
choices.D: It removes the need to measure the resulting expression levels.
choices.E: It makes the library uniform in strength rather than spread across a range.

library_construction_methods.explanation: A weight matrix records which bases appear at which positions among sequences that are known to function, so a code drawn from it biases the library toward that region of sequence space. The payoff is efficiency: a greater fraction of the clones you pick are worth measuring. A overstates it, since a matrix is a statistical summary and not a guarantee. C is wrong, as constraining positions lowers diversity rather than raising it. D is wrong because the point is still to measure. E is backwards, since a spread of strengths is the goal.

library_construction_methods.topic: Checking that designed diversity survives the construction
library_construction_methods.question: Your degenerate bases sit in the 5' tail of a primer, upstream of the restriction site used to clone the product. What happens to the library?

choices.A: Nothing; tails are retained in the final construct.
choices.B: The diversity is cut away with the flank during the digest, leaving a non-library product.
choices.C: The diversity moves into the vector backbone rather than the insert.
choices.D: The diversity is retained but inverted relative to the design.
choices.E: The diversity doubles, since both orientations of the tail are cloned.

library_construction_methods.explanation: A restriction digest discards everything outside the recognition site, including the short flank that was there to let the enzyme cut. Degenerate bases placed outside the site therefore end up in the discarded fragment, and every clone is identical. This is a real design error and the reason the degenerate region in a working oligo sits between the site and the annealing region. A ignores what the digest removes. C, D and E describe rearrangements that do not occur.

library_construction_methods.topic: Deciding between pooled and arrayed construction
library_construction_methods.question: You need twelve specific promoter variants, each one to be measured separately and kept as a named strain. Why would you build these one at a time rather than as a pooled degenerate library?

choices.A: Because degenerate synthesis cannot produce only twelve sequences.
choices.B: Because a pooled library would require deep sequencing to find and separate the twelve you wanted.
choices.C: Because pooled libraries cannot be transformed into competent cells.
choices.D: Because twelve variants exceed the diversity a single oligo can carry.
choices.E: Because named strains cannot be derived from a library by any means.

library_construction_methods.explanation: Pooling is worth the trouble when the number of variants is larger than you can handle individually. At twelve, building each on purpose gives you identified strains immediately, whereas pooling means screening or sequencing to work out which clone is which and then isolating them. A is essentially true as stated but is not the operative reason, since a small pool of defined oligos could be ordered. C and E are false. D inverts the scale problem.

library_construction_methods.topic: Matching the synthesis route to the kind of variation wanted
library_construction_methods.question: You want to test forty orthologs of one enzyme, each a different natural sequence of about 1.2 kb. What is the appropriate construction route?

choices.A: A degenerate oligo covering the positions at which the orthologs differ.
choices.B: Chip-based synthesis of the forty genes, amplified from the pool and assembled individually.
choices.C: Error-prone PCR of the host's own copy at a high mutation rate.
choices.D: EIPCR with a degenerate primer at the active site.
choices.E: A Klenow fill-in of forty annealed oligo pairs.

library_construction_methods.explanation: Forty full-length genes are forty defined sequences, which is the case chip synthesis exists to serve: the genes are written on a microarray, released as a pool, and selectively amplified and assembled. A is unworkable because orthologs differ at hundreds of positions in combinations that degenerate codes cannot specify. C and D generate variation around one sequence rather than reproducing forty real ones. E is limited to short cassettes, far shorter than a 1.2 kb gene.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Predicting the phenotype distribution a library produces
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: You place a library of ribosome binding sites upstream of a reporter gene in E. coli and plate the transformants. What is the most likely outcome?

choices.A: Every clone expresses the reporter at the same level but reaches it at a different time.
choices.B: The clones span a range of reporter levels across the population.
choices.C: Only clones with a strong ribosome binding site express at all, because the promoter represses the rest.
choices.D: The clones differ in plasmid copy number rather than in reporter level.
choices.E: The reporter level is unchanged, because the ribosome binding site acts on transcription.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: Changing the ribosome binding site changes how efficiently ribosomes initiate on the message, so the library produces a spread of protein levels. That spread is the product, which is why these libraries are built. A substitutes timing for level with no mechanism. C invents repression that is not in the design. D confuses a translational element with the origin of replication. E misassigns the ribosome binding site to transcription.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Matching a genetic element to the step it controls
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: A promoter library and a ribosome binding site library both give a range of protein output. At which step does each act?

choices.A: Both act on transcription, differing only in magnitude.
choices.B: The promoter library acts on transcription; the ribosome binding site library acts on translation initiation.
choices.C: The promoter library acts on translation; the ribosome binding site library acts on mRNA stability.
choices.D: Both act on translation, since protein is the readout in each case.
choices.E: The promoter library acts on copy number; the ribosome binding site library acts on transcription.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: The promoter determines how often RNA polymerase initiates, so a promoter library varies the amount of message. The ribosome binding site determines how readily the ribosome loads onto that message, so an RBS library varies protein made per message. Both end up changing protein, which is why D is tempting, but the step being varied is what the question asks. A, C and E each swap the two assignments or substitute copy number.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Choosing which element to vary for a stated goal
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: Two enzymes are expressed from one operon behind a single promoter, and you need more of the first and less of the second. Which change gives you that?

choices.A: Replace the promoter with a stronger one.
choices.B: Vary the ribosome binding site in front of the second gene.
choices.C: Move the operon to a higher copy number origin.
choices.D: Add a second copy of the promoter upstream of the operon.
choices.E: Change the codon usage of both genes together.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: Everything upstream of the operon acts on both genes at once, so a stronger promoter or a higher copy number raises both and leaves the ratio where it was. The ribosome binding site sits in front of one coding sequence and sets translation of that one, which is the only element in this list that can move the two independently. A, C and D all scale the pair. E acts on both genes and is a blunt instrument for level in any case.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Identifying the measured quantity for a terminator library
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: You build a library of terminator sequences between an upstream and a downstream fluorescent reporter. What does the experiment measure for each library member?

choices.A: The absolute brightness of the upstream reporter.
choices.B: The fraction of transcripts that read through the terminator, read as the ratio of downstream to upstream signal.
choices.C: The plasmid copy number of each clone.
choices.D: The rate at which the upstream reporter protein folds.
choices.E: The translation initiation rate of the downstream reporter.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: A terminator is judged by how much transcription it stops, and the way to see that without being confused by clone-to-clone differences in copy number or growth is to put a reporter on each side and take a ratio. The upstream reporter is the internal reference and the downstream one reports read-through. A would vary with copy number and growth rather than with the terminator. C, D and E name quantities the construct does not isolate.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Interpreting a library that produces no spread
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: You screen a ribosome binding site library in front of an enzyme and find that every clone gives the same pathway output. Which explanation is most plausible?

choices.A: The ribosome binding site does not affect translation in E. coli.
choices.B: The enzyme is not the step limiting pathway output, so changing its level changes nothing downstream.
choices.C: The library has no diversity, since identical output implies identical sequence.
choices.D: The reporter must be measured by cytometry rather than a plate reader.
choices.E: The promoter must have been deleted during cloning.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: The library almost certainly produced a range of enzyme levels; what the experiment shows is that pathway output does not respond to that range, which is what it looks like when some other step is the bottleneck. A contradicts the premise of the method. C is the right thing to check but the wrong inference, since sequencing would settle it and identical output has an easier explanation. D changes the instrument, not the result, for a bulk pathway measurement. E would abolish output rather than fix it at one level.

what_an_element_library_tunes.question: You move a reporter construct from a p15A origin to a high-copy origin and the signal rises fourfold. Your colleague concludes the promoter is stronger. What is wrong with that?

choices.A: Nothing; promoter strength and copy number are the same quantity.
choices.B: Copy number multiplies everything on the plasmid, so per-template initiation rate is unchanged.
choices.C: High-copy origins silence promoters, so the signal should have fallen.
choices.D: The comparison is invalid because fluorescence cannot be compared between strains.
choices.E: The promoter is weaker, since the same output is now spread over more templates.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: Promoter strength is a property of one template: how often polymerase initiates there. Raising copy number gives you more templates, each initiating at the same rate, so total output rises while the promoter is untouched. This is the distinction every expression comparison depends on. A collapses two different quantities. C invents an effect. D is too strong, since the comparison is routine with proper normalization. E confuses total with per-template but draws the opposite wrong conclusion.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Treating a library as a distribution to be sampled
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: A colleague says the purpose of a ribosome binding site library is to find the strongest ribosome binding site. What is the better description of what the library gives you?

choices.A: A distribution of expression levels, from which the screen picks whichever level the application needs.
choices.B: A single optimal sequence, which sequencing of the pool reveals directly.
choices.C: A measurement of the maximum expression the host can sustain.
choices.D: A set of clones all at the same level, differing only in sequence.
choices.E: A prediction of expression level from sequence, usable without any measurement.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: The library is a population spanning a range, and what counts as the best member depends on the goal: a pathway enzyme may need a middling level, and a toxic product may need a weak one. Treating the library as a search for a maximum discards most of its value. B is wrong because sequencing the pool tells you what is there, not what works. C is a different experiment. D contradicts the method. E describes a model, which libraries are used to build rather than to replace.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Recognizing survivor bias in a recovered library
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: You build a ribosome binding site library in front of a gene whose product is toxic above a certain level, transform, and grow the transformants overnight before picking. What does the recovered library look like relative to the one you designed?

choices.A: Unchanged, since toxicity affects growth rate rather than survival.
choices.B: Depleted of the strongest members, because those clones grow poorly or not at all.
choices.C: Depleted of the weakest members, because they are outcompeted.
choices.D: Enriched for the strongest members, since high expression gives a selective advantage.
choices.E: Unchanged in composition but uniformly lower in copy number.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: Overnight outgrowth is a selection whether or not you intended one. Clones expressing the toxic product most strongly divide slowly or die, so the high end of the designed distribution is thinned out or missing from what you pick. This is the same logic as plasmid loss under antibiotic: the population you measure is the population that survived the measurement. A understates it, since a growth-rate difference over many generations becomes a composition difference. C and D have the direction backwards. E invents an unrelated effect.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Choosing a tuning handle with a predictable effect
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: You need to tune the level of one enzyme across a wide range. Why is a ribosome binding site library a better handle than recoding the gene with alternative synonymous codons?

choices.A: Codon changes cannot alter protein level at all.
choices.B: The ribosome binding site is a small, separable element whose variation spans a wide range without touching the protein sequence.
choices.C: Codon changes require chip synthesis, which is unavailable for genes this size.
choices.D: The ribosome binding site determines the protein's folding, which codons do not.
choices.E: Synonymous codon changes alter the amino acid sequence and so confound the result.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: Varying a short element upstream of the start codon gives a broad, roughly monotonic range of initiation rates while leaving the coding sequence untouched, which keeps the enzyme itself out of the comparison. Recoding does shift expression, but through several entangled mechanisms including message structure and elongation, and across the whole gene. A and E are false; synonymous changes do affect expression and by definition do not change the protein. C is false. D misattributes folding to the ribosome binding site.

what_an_element_library_tunes.topic: Controlling the context around a varied part
what_an_element_library_tunes.question: In the course's terminator work, each candidate terminator is cloned into the same position in the same reporter plasmid rather than tested in whatever vector it arrived in. Why does that matter?

choices.A: It raises the theoretical diversity of the library.
choices.B: It keeps everything other than the part under test identical, so differences in signal can be assigned to the part.
choices.C: It is required for the parts to be sequenced by cycle sequencing.
choices.D: It increases the copy number of the construct and so the signal.
choices.E: It eliminates the need for an upstream reference reporter.

what_an_element_library_tunes.explanation: A part's measured behavior depends on its surroundings: promoter, copy number, growth, and the reporters on either side. Putting every candidate into one fixed context makes the measurements comparable with each other, which is the whole premise of characterizing parts. A has nothing to do with it. C is false. D is incidental and not the reason. E is backwards, since the internal reference is still needed to handle clone-to-clone variation.
